question: Several ongoing EU initiatives – including the European digital identity wallet, digital travel credentials, border databases, and platform obligations under the Digital Services Act1 – increasingly rely on cross-system interoperability.

If the Digital Omnibus weakens the constraints placed on secondary use or data repurposing by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)2, these interconnected systems may allow cross-database profiling or behavioural inference that current legislation was not designed to permit. 1.

What concrete safeguards will the Commission introduce to prevent cross-system profiling or inference between identity, travel, communication or platform datasets if GDPR restrictions on secondary processing are relaxed?
Will the Commission commit to a cumulative fundamental rights assessment explaining how GDPR relaxation affects the entire digital governance architecture, not only AIspecific use cases?

How will the Commission ensure that interoperability initiatives cannot be used to justify broader data flows under a more permissive interpretation of necessity, proportionality or public-interest grounds?

Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on a Single Market For Digital Services and amending Directive 2000/31/EC (Digital Services Act) (OJ L 277, 27.10.2022, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj).

Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation) (OJ L 119, 4.5.2016, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj).
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.1.2026) The Commission proposed well-targeted amendments to the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)12. They do not touch on the fundamentals of the GDPR but aim to harmonise, clarify, and simplify its application, and do not negatively impact individuals’ fundamental rights, including their right to data protection.

The proposed amendments are fully compliant with the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights3 and, for some parts, codify the existing case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union.4 They help controllers to better understand GDPR requirements and should therefore lead to improved data protection.

They reflect the findings of the Commission in the GDPR Implementation Dialogue and the second report on the application of the GDPR5. The proposal for a Digital Omnibus is accompanied by a Staff Working Document6 presenting the assessment of the impacts expected from the proposed amendments.

One of the amendments clarifies the compatibility of further processing of personal data for certain privileged purposes currently set out in Article 5(1)(b) GDPR, like scientific or historic research. The envisaged clarification is not applicable to any other purposes.

The proposed amendments do not in any way permit profiling across various services and systems nor alter specific rules in other EU laws, such as the rules in Regulation (EU) 910/2014 limiting the use of personal data across various services7, the prohibition under Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 on providers of online platforms to present advertisements based on profiling using special categories of personal data or personal data when the recipient of the service is a minor8, the data protection rules applicable to large-scale IT systems9, those set-out in the Interoperability Regulations10 and in the Commission’s proposal on digital travel credentials11.
